'''Michael Dudley Sturge''' (25 May 1931 – 13 July 2003) was an English experimental [[physicist]] best known for his contributions to solid-state [[spectroscopy]]. 

He was born in [[Bristol]] to a family with a [[Quakers|Quaker tradition]] and educated at [[Leighton Park School]] and [[Cambridge University]]. 
<ref name="ptobit">{{cite journal | last=Rashba | first=Emmanuel | last2=Stormer | first2=Horst | last3=Cohen | first3=Elisha | last4=Hegarty | first4=John | title=Michael Dudley Sturge | journal=Physics Today | publisher=AIP Publishing | volume=57 | issue=7 | year=2004 | issn=0031-9228 | doi=10.1063/1.1784318 | pages=79–80| doi-access=free }}</ref> While his most influential paper is about discovery of [[exciton]]s in [[gallium arsenide]],<ref>{{cite journal | last=Sturge | first=M. D. | title=Optical Absorption of Gallium Arsenide between 0.6 and 2.75 eV | journal=Physical Review | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=127 | issue=3 | date=1962-08-01 | issn=0031-899X | doi=10.1103/physrev.127.768 | pages=768–773}}</ref> the scope of his research covered wide field of solid-state spectroscopy, and its impact is reflected by establishment of the Sturge Prize in condensed matter spectroscopy.
<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.canterbury.ac.nz/conferences/dpc19/Prizes |title = DPC19}}</ref>

After accepting the editorship of the ''[[Journal of Luminescence]]'' in 1985, Sturge drastically extended its scope by transforming it into a journal covering the extensive area of the contemporary condensed matter spectroscopy. He stepped down as chief editor in 1990.<ref name="ptobit"/> He died in Castleton, England on 13 July 2003, of leukaemia.<ref name="ptobit"/>

Sturge's achievements have been recognized by establishment of the ''Sturge Prize'' for scientists at the initial phase of their scientific career by the International Conference on Dynamical Processes in Excited States of Solids. The prize was first awarded in 2005.<ref name="ptobit"/>
